claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlegel and Schuster, 2008 and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In contrast to male hoverflies, ecological constraints in archerfish do not allow similar simplifying assumptions.
claims.source: In contrast to the conditions in the male hoverfly, the ecological constraints in archerfish do not allow similar simplifying assumptions and archerfish can respond appropriately from a large range of distances and initial orientation and when encountering targets of unusual size or speed (as will be shown below).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B, with supporting data to be shown later.

claims.claim: Archerfish shoot down aerial prey with jets of water.
claims.source: This decision is an essential part of the hunting behavior of archerfish, in which the fish shoot down aerial prey with jets of water (Dill, 1977; Schuster, 2018; Gerullis and Schuster, 2014; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Once prey is dislodged, archerfish have only the little time remaining until prey hits the water surface to turn and dash off to be at the impact point just when prey arrives.
claims.source: Once a prey insect is successfully dislodged, shooters and bystander archerfish have only the little time that remains till prey hits the water surface to turn and dash off to be at the impact point of prey just when it arrives there.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a description of the hunting behavior.

claims.claim: In the wild, missing the impact point or not being there in time would typically mean losing prey to more numerous competing surface-feeding fish.
claims.source: In the wild, missing this point or not being there in time, would typically mean losing prey to the more numerous competing other surface-feeding fish (Rischawy et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rischawy et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Archerfish watch the initial movement of dislodged prey and then quickly and accurately select the appropriate turn and take-off to be at the later landing point at the right time.
claims.source: The solution archerfish have evolved to secure their prey and to outperform their competitors is to watch the initial movement of dislodged prey and then quickly and accurately select the appropriate turn and take-off to be at the later landing point at the right time (e.g., Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002; Schuster, 2023; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Archerfish predictive C-starts are among the fastest C-starts known in fish.
claims.source: Their so-called predictive C-start decisions are among the fastest C-starts known in fish and are initiated much faster than an Olympic sprinter can respond to the start gun (Sillar et al., 2016; see Video 1 for an appreciation of the decision's speed).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Sillar et al., 2016 and Video 1.

claims.claim: When archerfish were challenged with prey that was prevented from falling but only slid on a glass plate, they still responded with turns toward the appropriate virtual ballistic impact points.
claims.source: When many such interspersed rare cases with sliding flies were later analyzed, it turned out that fish still responded, although nothing fell. Moreover, their response latency – measured between the onset of prey motion and the onset of the turns – was the same as in most tests in which real prey was falling (Rossel et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rossel et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: For each set of conditions with sliding flies, the fish turned to the appropriate virtual impact point calculated based on ballistics.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that for each set of conditions the fish had turned to the appropriate virtual impact point, calculated based on ballistics, just as they would toward a real later impact point of real falling prey (Rossel et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Rossel et al., 2002 and illustrated in Figure 2A, B.

claims.claim: The archerfish decision circuit maps the initial values of motion to the turn angle needed to reach the ballistic landing point.
claims.source: This implies that the fish were able to map the initial values of motion to the turn angle they needed to produce and that this mapping is appropriate for ballistically falling objects (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results illustrated in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Archerfish turn decisions exclusively use information sampled during a brief interval after onset of prey motion.
claims.source: The archerfish's turn decisions exclusively use information that is sampled during a brief interval after onset of prey motion (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Reinel and Schuster, 2014; Reinel and Schuster, 2018a; Reinel and Schuster, 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The information used in archerfish turn decisions includes the initial height from which prey is falling.
claims.source: This information even includes the initial height from which prey is falling (Reinel and Schuster, 2018a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Reinel and Schuster, 2018a.

claims.claim: All experiments have shown that the archerfish start decision does not use or has no access to prior information.
claims.source: In other words, all experiments available have shown that the start decision does not use or has no access to prior information. Instead, it relies exclusively on information sampled once prey starts moving.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a summary of previous experimental findings.

claims.claim: All archerfish studied in the lab and in the wild consistently showed robust turn decisions towards the inferred ballistic landing points.
claims.source: Because all archerfish studied so far in the lab and in the wild consistently showed robust turn decisions towards the inferred ballistic landing points (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002; Rischawy et al., 2015; Reinel and Schuster, 2014; Reinel and Schuster, 2018a; Reinel and Schuster, 2018b; Wöhl and Schuster, 2006; Wöhl and Schuster, 2007), we expected the decision to be hardwired to ballistics.
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Hardwiring the decision circuit to ballistic falling patterns could be fixed genetically and/or established during the early ontogeny of the fish.
claims.source: Hardwiring the decision circuit to ballistic falling patterns could be fixed genetically and/or established during the early ontogeny of the fish.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis.

claims.claim: An initial aim to the ballistic landing point would be in error for non-ballistically falling prey, but this initial error could be corrected during the actual approach trajectory.
claims.source: While an initial aim to the ballistic landing point would be in error for non-ballistically falling prey, this initial error of the fish's turn could always be corrected during the actual approach trajectory.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about potential alternative strategies.

claims.claim: Adult archerfish are capable of learning to extract and use a novel non-ballistic rule of how to connect the three independent input variables of prey motion to the point to which they must turn to receive a reward.
claims.source: Nevertheless, we demonstrate here that the decision is not hardwired to ballistic falling. We show that adult archerfish are capable of learning to extract and to use a novel non-ballistic rule of how to connect the three independent input variables of prey motion to the point to which they must turn to receive a reward.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: A virtual reality system was developed that presents information with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution as needed by the decision circuit.
claims.source: To be useful for the question at hand, the system needs to fulfill four conditions: (i) First, it must present the information with sufficient spatial and temporal resolution as needed by the decision circuit.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in the Results section.

claims.claim: The VR system presents the reward at the positions and times as required by ballistic or arbitrary other rules without adding further information that could interfere with the decision.
claims.source: (ii) Second, it needs to present the reward at the positions and times as required by ballistic or arbitrary other rules but without adding further information that could interfere with the decision.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The VR system works so well that there is no statistically detectable difference between virtual and real responses.
claims.source: (iii) Third, the VR system would have to work so well that there is no statistically detectable difference between virtual and real responses.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement and demonstrated in Figure 3C-G.

claims.claim: The VR system keeps the fish motivated for many months of experimentation during which the fish exclusively face virtual objects.
claims.source: (iv) Finally, the system must keep the fish motivated for the many months of experimentation during which the fish will exclusively be facing virtual objects.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a requirement and implicitly demonstrated by the long-term training data.

claims.claim: The successful VR setup used an LCD screen at a frame rate of 120 frames per second and employed custom-made automatic feeders.
claims.source: After several unsuccessful attempts – including LED-based arrangements used in earlier work (Strauss et al., 1997; Schuster et al., 2002; Reiser and Dickinson, 2008) – we found a system that completely fulfilled all four crucial conditions. In the following, we present evidence for that successful system (Figure 3). The setup worked, surprisingly, with an LCD screen at a frame rate of 120 frames per second and employed custom-made automatic feeders that were non-transparent and provided food at the right time and place, coupled to the motion shown on the screen.
claims.evidence: This is described in the Methods and illustrated in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The VR setup readily and continuously elicited turns toward the calculated ballistic impact point.
claims.source: First, the setup readily and continuously elicited turns toward the calculated ballistic impact point (Figure 3B–G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B-G.

claims.claim: Operating the feeders without showing motion on the screen failed to elicit turn decisions.
claims.source: Operating the feeders without showing motion on the screen failed to elicit turn decisions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: When feeders were placed systematically offset from the ballistic virtual impact points, turns were aimed at the VIPs and not at the feeders.
claims.source: Most importantly, when feeders were placed not at the ballistic virtual impact points (VIPs) but systematically offset from them, then turns were aimed at the VIPs and not at the feeders – even though this was where the fish got their reward (Figure 3B; 15° offset, n=353; 30° offset, n=198).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: The decisions were only based on the movement information presented on the screen and were not influenced by cues from the feeders or from any other landmarks in the tank.
claims.source: In other words, even in the presence of the feeders were the decisions only based on the movement information that was presented on the screen and were not influenced by cues from the feeders or from any other landmarks in the tank.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: No aspect of the decisions was statistically different under real and virtual conditions.
claims.source: Given the limitations in the temporal resolution of the screen it is striking that no aspect of the decisions was statistically different under real and virtual conditions (Figure 3C–G, n=101 (real) and n=85 (virtual) starts).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C-G.

claims.claim: The accuracy of the aim was not statistically different between real and virtual conditions (p=0.506).
claims.source: The accuracy of the aim achieved at the end of the turns (measured as introduced in Figure 2) was not statistically different (p=0.506, Mann-Whitney; Figure 3C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Turns always minimized the error to the impact point, regardless of whether it was real or virtual.
claims.source: and always minimized the error to the impact point, regardless of whether it was real or virtual (difference from zero: p=0.903 (real), p=0.455 (virtual); One-Sample Signed Rank)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in variance between real and virtual conditions (p=0.589).
claims.source: with also no significant difference in variance (p=0.589, Brown-Forsythe).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The turns had the same latency between real and virtual conditions (p=0.297).
claims.source: The turns also had the same latency (between onset of prey motion and onset of the turns; p=0.297; Mann-Whitney; Figure 3D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: There was no difference in bending duration under real and VR conditions (p=0.071).
claims.source: and kinematics (Figure 3E: no difference in bending duration under real and VR conditions, p=0.071, Mann-Whitney).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Responses came from a large range of orientations and distances and were equally accurate across all distances and turn sizes.
claims.source: Furthermore, responses came from a large range of orientations and distances and, most importantly, were equally accurate across all distances (Figure 3F) and turn sizes (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3F and 3G.

claims.claim: The turn decisions were equivalent in all examined aspects (accuracy, latency, kinematics) to those obtained with real falling objects.
claims.source: In summary, despite the limited frame rate of the screens and despite the need to use highly conspicuous feeders in the majority of the (rewarded) presentations, the turn decisions were equivalent in all examined aspects (accuracy, latency, kinematics) to those obtained with real falling objects.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the data presented in Figure 3.

claims.claim: A new rule was introduced that generates a systematic and substantial deviation (of 14.9 cm) between the new VIPs and the ballistic VIPs.
claims.source: Figure 4A introduces the new rule that we chose to face the fish with. It generates a systematic and substantial deviation (of 14.9 cm) between the new VIPs and the ballistic VIPs as inferred from the initial movement.
claims.evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: After the new rule was introduced, the movement direction is deflected by 39.8° to the left after the fish's typical decision time.
claims.source: After having traveled straight throughout what was the previous decision time, the movement direction is deflected by 39.8° (to the left, s. Methods), and the reward is now presented at the appropriate 'deflected' VIP.
claims.evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: According to the new rule, the connection between initial movement and the point of reward is still precisely defined.
claims.source: According to this new rule, the connection between initial movement and the point of reward is still precisely defined.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a property of the new rule.

claims.claim: Learning to turn according to the new rule requires the fish to learn non-trivial corrections that depend sensitively on the position of the responding fish.
claims.source: It would require the fish to learn non-trivial corrections that can be appreciated by considering Figure 4B: Relative to the turn they had previously made for a given input constellation they would need to add a correction that is not constant but depends sensitively on the position of the responding fish.
claims.evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: A new map of corrections is required for every combination of input variables.
claims.source: This map of corrections is, furthermore, not the same for all input constellations. Instead, a new map of the kind shown in Figure 4B is required for every combination of input variables (as illustrated with a simple example in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is explained in the text and illustrated in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The fish never ceased to respond with their characteristic turns during training to the new rule.
claims.source: Interestingly, the fish never ceased to respond with their characteristic turns (response probability remained constant across all training blocks, p>0.08, Pairwise Chi-square).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the training data.

claims.claim: The kinematics of the turns and latency remained constant during training to the new rule.
claims.source: The kinematics of the turns and latency also remained constant (bending and straightening phase of their C-starts both p>0.28, latency p>0.07; Kruskal-Wallis).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the training data.

claims.claim: The aims were systematically in error for the initial training blocks.
claims.source: Furthermore, their aims were systematically in error for the initial training blocks (deviation from zero error to the deflected VIPs p≤0.001, One-Sample Signed Rank) as expected (Figure 4D; deviation of aim to ballistic VIPs from zero error p>0.06; One-Sample Signed Rank; Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4D and Video 3.

claims.claim: After more than 1750 presentations (55 experimental days), the turns clearly minimized the error to the appropriate new 'deflected' VIPs and no longer to the ballistic ones.
claims.source: However, gradually the errors made to the new 'deflected' VIPs became smaller and, after more than 1750 presentations (55 experimental days), the turns clearly minimized the error to the appropriate new 'deflected' VIPs (Figure 4C, E, F; Video 4) and no longer to the ballistic ones.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4C, E, F and Video 4.

claims.claim: In interspersed tests with only the initial linear part of motion shown, the errors made were not different from those made when the full trajectories were visible.
claims.source: The errors made in the interspersed tests (n=68) were not different from those made when the full trajectories were visible (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: In interspersed tests with only initial movement shown and direction offset from feeder positions, the turns were still aimed at the new deflected VIPs.
claims.source: Yet, the turns the fish made in these tests were still aimed at the new deflected VIPs (differences from zero error p=0.721 at 15° (n=197) and p=0.113 at 72° (n=145); One-Sample t-tests) but not at the feeders and also not at the ballistic VIPs (Kruskal-Wallis: p≤0.001 at 15°; p=0.005 at 72°; Dunn's p<0.05 for comparison of errors; Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4G and Video 5.

claims.claim: The turns made when only the linear initial motion was visible and when the VIPs were spatially offset from the feeders did not differ in latency or kinematics from the turns made without offset and with the full trajectory visible.
claims.source: Furthermore, the turns – made when only the linear initial motion was visible and when the VIPs were spatially offset from the feeders – did not differ in latency (p=0.686, Kruskal-Wallis) nor in kinematics (bending duration: p=0.242, Kruskal-Wallis) from the turns made without offset and with the full trajectory visible (n=240).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data related to Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The new turns were possible and equally accurate across a range of distances and turn angles.
claims.source: Finally, the new turns were not restricted to just a few positions and orientations of the responding fish. Rather, they were possible and equally accurate across a range of distances and turn angles (Figure 4H, I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4H and 4I.

claims.claim: There was no significant linear or Spearman correlation between error magnitude and response latency in the re-programmed decisions.
claims.source: For both plots, there was no significant linear (p=0.318, R2=0.005, Figure 4J; p=0.469, R2=0.004, Figure 4K) or Spearman correlation (p=0.128 and 0.174, respectively, in Figure 4J, K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 4J and 4K.

claims.claim: A highspeed decision that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff can be flexibly reprogrammed to a new rule.
claims.source: Our findings, therefore, demonstrate that a highspeed decision that lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff can be flexibly reprogrammed to a new rule.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: All training to the new rule was carried out exclusively with targets presented at only one height level.
claims.source: This can be examined conveniently because all training to the new rule was carried out exclusively with targets presented at only one height level.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental design feature.

claims.claim: Possible target speed levels were limited, and prey was of only one size during training.
claims.source: In addition, possible target speed levels were limited, and prey was of only one size.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an experimental design feature.

claims.claim: The turns already minimized the error to the VIPs that were appropriate for the untrained novel height levels right from the start with no trend that errors would decrease.
claims.source: Interestingly, the turns already minimized the error to the VIPs that were appropriate for the untrained novel height levels. They were appropriate right from start with no trend that errors would decrease (linear regression: all p>0.1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: The turns minimized the error to the deflected landing point also at the untrained height levels.
claims.source: A detailed analysis of the errors (Figure 5D, E) showed that the turns minimized the error to the deflected landing point also at the untrained height levels (difference from zero: both p>0.07; One-Sample t-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: The turns were not directed to the ballistic landing point (prediction 'ballistic') at untrained height levels.
claims.source: They were also not directed to the ballistic landing point (prediction 'ballistic;' both p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: The turns were not directed towards the deflected landing point at the training height (prediction 'substitute') at untrained height levels.
claims.source: and not towards the deflected landing point at the training height (prediction 'substitute;' both p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: None of the characteristics of the turns had changed in the novel situation compared to those after training.
claims.source: Again, none of the characteristics of the turns had changed in the novel situation compared to those after training (also n=30 right before these tests): latency: p=0.098, kinematics: p=0.177 (Kruskal-Wallis), variance of errors: p=0.188 (Brown-Forsythe).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing data before and after the height change.

claims.claim: The new rule is not represented by updating a simple lookup table but in a way that allows immediate generalization to new untrained height levels.
claims.source: In other words, the new rule is not represented by updating a simple lookup table but in a way that allows immediate generalization to the new untrained height levels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the generalization data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: When faced with a new absolute prey size, the trained fish immediately turned to the deflected landing points.
claims.source: Again, the trained fish immediately turned to the deflected landing points (differences from zero error: each p>0.4, One-Sample Signed Rank; difference in aim before and after size change p=0.764, Mann-Whitney)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Learning did not involve simplifying a priori assumptions about absolute prey size.
claims.source: Hence, learning did also not involve simplifying a priori assumptions about absolute prey size.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: When tests with lower than training speed were interspersed, the first 30 turns made at the lower speed minimized the error to the actual deflected VIP.
claims.source: When tests with lower than training speed were interspersed among presentations with the speed levels as during training, then already the first 30 turns made at the lower speed (Figure 5G) minimized the error to the actual deflected VIP (difference from zero p=0.102; One-Sample t-test)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: At untrained speed levels, turns did not minimize error to VIPs given by ballistics or by using predictions for the deflected VIPs based on the trained speed levels.
claims.source: but not to the VIPs given by either ballistics (prediction 'ballistic;' p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank) or by using predictions for the deflected VIPs that are based on the trained speed levels (p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Changing target size and speed did not affect the nature of the turns (latency, bending duration, variance of errors).
claims.source: Comparing latency, bending duration, and the variance of errors (speed: last 30 presentations with only training speed; size: last 30 presentations with target size during training) showed that changing target size and speed also did not affect the nature of the turns. Latency and bending duration were not significantly different in the changed versus training conditions (at novel untrained speed: Latency: p=0.280, Mann-Whitney; Stage 1: p=0.076, Mann-Whitney. At novel untrained size: Latency: p=0.305, t-test; Stage 1: p=0.997, Mann-Whitney). Variance was even slightly reduced (and not increased) at the untrained target speed (p=0.021, Brown-Forsythe) and remained unchanged after the increase in target size (p=0.742, Brown-Forsythe).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: All tests show that the decisions had been reprogrammed in much more clever ways than predicted, allowing immediate generalization.
claims.source: In summary, all tests show that the decisions had been reprogrammed in much more clever ways than predicted. Rather than independently changing the size of an unrewarding turn for each individual constellation – as would seem required because the input variables themselves are varied independently from each other – learning allowed immediate generalization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on all the generalization data in Figure 5.

claims.claim: When trained fish were randomly shown two differently shaped objects (disk and triangle), the turns made in response to the 'ballistic object' initially still minimized the error to the deflected VIP.
claims.source: However, in experiments to test this prediction, the turns made in response to the 'ballistic object' (rewarded at the ballistic VIP) initially still minimized the error to the deflected VIP (difference from zero error p=0.256; One-Sample Signed Rank; same variance as for disk p=0.343; Brown-Forsythe; first 160 responses to ballistic object) and not to the ballistic VIP point (difference to ballistic landing point: p=0.038, Mann-Whitney; Figure 6B, C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B and 6C.

claims.claim: After 500 additional starts in response to the ballistic objects, turns were equally in error to the deflected and the ballistic VIPs.
claims.source: However, after 500 additional starts in response to the ballistic objects, turns were equally in error to the deflected and the ballistic VIPs (p=0.648, Mann-Whitney).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The turns made to the moving disks remained unaffected throughout the same period and remained perfectly matched to the deflected landing point.
claims.source: In contrast, the turns made to the moving disks remained unaffected throughout the same period and remained perfectly matched to the deflected landing point (difference from zero error p=0.273; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: After about 300 additional encounters of moving triangles, the turns minimized the error to the ballistic impact point when a triangle was shown.
claims.source: After about 300 additional encounters of moving triangles the turns minimized the error to the ballistic impact point when a triangle was shown (error to ballistic VIPs p=0.836, error to deflected VIPs p=0.020; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The turns continued to minimize the error to the deflected impact point whenever the disk was shown.
claims.source: However, the turns continued to minimize the error to the deflected impact point whenever the disk was shown (error to ballistic p≤0.001, error to deflected p=0.084, n=187; One-Sample Signed Rank; Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: In interspersed tests with only the initial straight paths shown for both disk and triangle, the turns were toward the ballistic landing point when the triangle was shown and to the deflected landing point when the disk was shown.
claims.source: Again, the turns were toward the ballistic landing point when the triangle was shown (difference from ballistic p=0.075, from deflected p<0.001; One-Sample Signed Rank) and to the deflected landing point when the disk was shown (difference from ballistic p=0.008, from deflected p=0.412; One-Sample Signed Rank) (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Latency and kinematics of the turns were the same in the responses to triangles and disks.
claims.source: Also, latency (p=0.189, Mann-Whitney; Figure 6E) and kinematics of the turns (bending duration; p=0.984; Mann-Whitney; Figure 6F) were the same in the responses to triangles and disks.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6E and 6F.

claims.claim: Object shape determined which rule the decision used to determine the appropriate turn given the input data.
claims.source: In other words, the nature of the turn decision was the same, but object shape determined which rule the decision used to determine the appropriate turn given the input data.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6D-F.

claims.claim: All three individual fish that contributed most of the starts minimized the error to the appropriate VIP.
claims.source: Our analysis showed that all three of the three individual fish that had contributed most of the starts in Figure 6 minimized the error to the appropriate VIP (Figure 6G; difference from zero error always p>0.1; One-Sample Signed Rank).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The variability of the errors in applying the two rules did not differ in any of the individuals.
claims.source: Also, the variability of the errors in applying the two rules did also not differ in any of the individuals (p=0.966; Brown-Forsythe).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The decision circuit used by archerfish has the potential of simultaneously operating on two different rules.
claims.source: This shows clearly that the decision circuit used by archerfish does have the potential of simultaneously operating on two different rules.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 6.

claims.claim: In tests where the prey object revealed its shape only at motion onset, the decisions remained appropriate to the ballistic or deflected VIPs.
claims.source: Under these conditions, the decisions remained appropriate to the ballistic (triangle; n=109 starts) or deflected (disk; n=46 starts) VIPs (difference from zero error to appropriate VIP: p=0.451 (triangle) and p=0.671 (disk); p≤0.001 for the alternatives, all One-Sample Signed Rank).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The distribution of errors was not statistically different when shape cue was available 2 s prior versus only during the decision phase.
claims.source: Furthermore, also the distribution of errors was not statistically different from those obtained with the shape cue available 2 s prior to the decision (p=0.269; Brown-Forsythe).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The information needed to select which rule is to be used can be extracted in the very brief interval after motion onset, together with all other decision-relevant information.

results.result: A virtual reality (VR) system was developed and validated that presents visual stimuli on an LCD screen at 120 fps with automatic feeders delivering rewards at virtual impact points. The system elicits turn decisions that are statistically indistinguishable from those elicited by real falling objects in all measured aspects including accuracy, latency, and kinematics.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C65 collectively demonstrate that the VR system meets all four stated requirements and produces decisions equivalent to real conditions. Statistical comparisons (C59-C63) show no significant differences (p>0.05) between virtual and real conditions across multiple parameters. Critical control experiments (C55-C57) confirm decisions are based solely on screen motion, not feeder positions or other cues.

results.result: Adult archerfish successfully reprogrammed their highspeed decision to a new non-ballistic rule after training with deflected trajectories. After more than 1750 presentations over 55 days, fish turned toward the new deflected virtual impact points rather than ballistic ones, even when only initial motion was shown and feeders were spatially offset.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C48, C66-C80 provide converging evidence for reprogramming. Training data (C71-C74) show systematic error reduction over time with maintained response characteristics. Critical tests with only initial motion shown and offset feeders (C75-C76) demonstrate the decision was based on the new rule, not visual feedback or feeder positions. Statistical tests confirm turns minimized error to deflected VIPs (p>0.1) but not to ballistic VIPs or feeders (p≤0.005).

results.result: After reprogramming to the deflected rule, fish immediately generalized to untrained conditions including novel height levels, prey sizes, and speed levels without additional training. Turns were accurate from the first presentations at untrained conditions with no improvement trend, ruling out simple lookup table mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C81-C94 demonstrate immediate generalization across multiple untrained dimensions. Statistical analyses (C84-C86, C89, C91-C92) show turns minimized error to appropriate deflected VIPs at novel conditions (p>0.07) but not to predictions based on ballistics or training-height substitution (p<0.001). The absence of learning curves (C83) and maintained response characteristics (C87, C93) support genuine abstraction rather than memorization.

results.result: The decision circuit can simultaneously operate on two distinct rules, using ballistic predictions for triangular objects and deflected predictions for disk-shaped objects. Individual fish demonstrated this dual-rule capability with equivalent accuracy and response characteristics for both object types.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C95-C105 demonstrate simultaneous dual-rule operation. After training with both object types, fish turned to ballistic VIPs for triangles and deflected VIPs for disks (C98-C99, p<0.05). Critical tests with only initial motion shown (C100) confirmed shape-based rule selection. Individual fish analysis (C103-C104) rules out group-level explanations, showing all three top contributors used both rules with equivalent accuracy (p>0.1) and variance (p=0.966).

results.result: Shape information needed to select between rules can be extracted during the brief decision phase after motion onset, without requiring prior information. Decisions remained accurate when shape was revealed only at motion onset rather than 2 seconds before.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 show rule selection does not require prior information. When shape was revealed only at motion onset, decisions remained appropriate to the correct VIPs (p>0.4) with error distributions statistically indistinguishable from conditions with 2s prior shape information (p=0.269, C107). This demonstrates rule selection occurs within the <100ms decision window.

results.result: The archerfish highspeed decision lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff both before and after reprogramming, with decisions made in less than 100ms. This provides a counterexample to the view that highspeed decisions necessarily lack flexibility and rely on simplifying heuristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C79, C110, C115, C120, C147 establish the absence of speed-accuracy tradeoff. Statistical analyses (C79) show no significant correlation between error magnitude and response latency in reprogrammed decisions (p>0.3, R²<0.005). Combined with demonstrated flexibility (reprogramming, generalization, dual-rule operation), this challenges the prevailing view that highspeed decisions must be inflexible (C3, C22-C25).

results.result: Archerfish turn toward virtual ballistic impact points calculated from initial prey motion even when prey does not actually fall, demonstrating the decision circuit maps initial motion parameters to appropriate turn angles based on ballistic trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 establish the baseline ballistic mapping behavior that forms the foundation for the reprogramming experiments. Prior work (Rossel et al., 2002) demonstrated fish turn to calculated virtual impact points when prey slides rather than falls, with consistent findings across lab and wild populations. This provides the critical baseline showing the decision was initially tuned to ballistics.

results.result: The prevailing view in the field is that highspeed decisions that lack speed-accuracy tradeoffs achieve speed through simplifying heuristics that work for common conditions but lack flexibility for variable conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C9-C12, C21-C25 establish the theoretical framework and prevailing view that the study challenges. These claims are supported by multiple citations to established literature (Chittka et al., 2009; Gladwell, 2005; Gigerenzer, 2007; Collett and Land, 1978) and represent the consensus view that motivates the research question.

results.result: Multiple examples across species demonstrate rapid decisions without speed-accuracy tradeoffs, including rat odor discrimination (~300ms), archerfish prey interception, human visual categorization (20-40ms), and baseball hitting decisions (~70ms visual processing).
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 provide empirical examples supporting the existence of rapid decisions without speed-accuracy tradeoffs. Each claim is supported by appropriate citations to peer-reviewed literature. These examples establish that the phenomenon exists across diverse species and sensory modalities, providing context for the archerfish study.

results.result: Male hoverflies use a hardwired rapid interception strategy based on fixed assumptions about female speed, size, and male acceleration. When challenged with objects deviating from these assumptions, they make predictable errors, exemplifying a fast but inflexible decision.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 describe the hoverfly interception behavior as a canonical example of an inflexible highspeed decision. This is well-supported by citation to Collett and Land (1978) and serves as a useful contrast to the archerfish findings. The hoverfly example illustrates the type of hardwired, inflexible system the authors initially expected to find in archerfish.

results.result: Archerfish use predictive C-starts to intercept falling prey, initiating turns in as little as 40ms based on initial prey motion (speed, height, direction). These are among the fastest C-starts known in fish, faster than Olympic sprinter reaction times, and are crucial for outcompeting other surface-feeding fish.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C38 establish the biological context and characteristics of archerfish hunting behavior. These claims are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work (Schlegel and Schuster, 2008; Rossel et al., 2002; Schuster, 2023; Rischawy et al., 2015) and provide essential background for understanding the decision system being studied.

results.result: The authors initially hypothesized that the archerfish decision circuit might be hardwired to ballistics through genetic or early developmental mechanisms, though initial errors could potentially be corrected during approach trajectories.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 present the authors' initial hypotheses that motivated the study. These are clearly labeled as hypotheses/speculation and represent reasonable predictions based on prior observations (C45) showing consistent ballistic responses across all tested fish. The hypotheses provide important context for why the reprogramming results are surprising.

results.result: The cognitive aspects demonstrated (generalization, abstraction, dual-rule operation) are not unique to archerfish and have been shown in other species. What is surprising is finding these features in a decision made at reflex-like speed (<100ms) without speed-accuracy tradeoff.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C122 provide important context for interpreting the significance of the findings. The authors appropriately acknowledge that individual cognitive features are not novel (supported by citations C117-C119), but emphasize that the combination of these features with reflex-like speed is unexpected. This framing is well-supported and helps clarify the study's contribution.

results.result: The assumption that reflex speed implies reduced complexity may be analogous to the now-challenged assumption that smaller brains have reduced cognitive capacity. Evidence from insects and other small-brained animals demonstrates sophisticated cognitive abilities despite minimal neural resources.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C129 draw an analogy between brain size and processing speed as potential constraints on cognitive complexity. This analogy is well-supported by extensive citations to literature on insect cognition (Chittka and Niven, 2009; Giurfa, 2013; Roussel et al., 2012) and provides a useful conceptual framework for interpreting the findings.

results.result: Archerfish predictive C-starts share kinematics with escape C-starts and are among the fastest C-starts in fish. The motor circuits are likely restricted to hindbrain circuits organized around the Mauthner neuron, though other hindbrain neurons are needed for precision.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C133 provide neurobiological context for the decision system. These claims are well-supported by citations to prior work (Wöhl and Schuster, 2007; Korn and Faber, 2005; Machnik et al., 2018a,b; Hecker et al., 2020) and help explain how a 'functional minibrain' might implement the observed cognitive flexibility.

results.result: The study analyzed six fish that reached homogeneous performance levels. While individual learning speeds may vary, demonstrating reprogramming in even one fish illustrates the circuit's potential capabilities. The possibility of observational or social learning remains unexplored.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C137 address potential limitations regarding sample size and individual variation. The authors appropriately acknowledge these limitations while defending their approach with a reasonable analogy (C134). The acknowledgment of unexplored possibilities (C137) is appropriately speculative and suggests future directions.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that decision flexibility evolved due to competition with other surface-feeding fish and the need to handle prey of varying sizes that fall with different trajectories due to air resistance. Hardwired ballistic-only responses would produce errors for larger prey requiring time-costly corrections.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C146 present ecological hypotheses for why flexibility might have evolved. While the competitive context is supported by citation (C140: Rischawy et al., 2015), the specific evolutionary scenario is explicitly speculative (C146: 'clearly without proof'). The physics of air resistance affecting larger prey (C143) is sound, but direct evidence that wild archerfish encounter prey with systematically different falling patterns is not provided.

results.result: The findings raise questions about whether highspeed decision flexibility is widespread, what factors drive speed-accuracy tradeoffs in most decisions, and suggest potential technological applications for rapid flexible decision-making systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C150 appropriately identify future research directions and potential applications arising from the findings. These are clearly framed as open questions and possibilities rather than established conclusions, which is appropriate for a discussion section.

results.result: Experiments used six adult archerfish in a 1m×1m×0.6m tank with an LCD monitor (120 fps) presenting stimuli with 0.96 Michelson contrast. Ballistic trajectories moved at 1.775 m/s for 243ms; deflected trajectories changed direction by 39.8° after 116ms. Only first-responding fish were analyzed to avoid social influence.
results.evaluation: Claims C151-C164 describe methodological details that are clearly stated and internally consistent. The experimental parameters are precisely specified with appropriate units and measurements. The decision to analyze only first responders (C162) is well-justified given the group context requirement (C161).

results.result: The authors developed a virtual reality (VR) system that successfully replicates real prey capture conditions for archerfish. The VR system presents visual stimuli with sufficient temporal and spatial resolution, elicits turns toward calculated ballistic impact points, and produces decisions that are statistically indistinguishable from those made with real falling objects in terms of accuracy, latency, and kinematics.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raised critical concerns about the VR system's technical adequacy, noting that the 120 FPS frame rate produces 15 mm jumps per frame at the target speed, questioning whether this constitutes 'continuous motion' and whether the fish truly perceive virtual targets as falling. The reviewer stated 'the experimental setup is not well designed' and questioned validation of fish perception. However, after revision, the reviewer acknowledged 'the authors handled the comments, and the manuscript has improved accordingly,' though noting 'some issues could still benefit from further clarification.' The editor and other reviewers found the VR system 'sophisticated and clever' with 'robust controls,' but the initial methodological concerns were significant enough to create uncertainty about this foundational result.

results.result: Adult archerfish can reprogram their high-speed decision-making to follow a novel non-ballistic rule in which the landing point is deflected 39.8° from the ballistic prediction. After training with over 1750 presentations (55 days), fish accurately turned toward the new deflected virtual impact points rather than ballistic ones, even when only initial motion was shown and feeders were spatially offset. The reprogrammed decisions maintained the same speed and lacked a speed-accuracy tradeoff.
results.evaluation: The editor and Reviewer 3 found the reprogramming results convincing and important, with the editor stating the data are 'convincing' and Reviewer 3 calling it a 'remarkable finding.' However, Reviewer 2 challenged a foundational claim, arguing that 'the argument that the fish can modulate reflex-like behavior relies on the claim that the archerfish makes the decision in 40 ms' but 'there is little support for the 40 ms reaction time,' citing previous studies showing 60-75 ms latencies. The reviewer stated this is 'critical for the analysis' because 'if the reaction time is longer, maybe this is not a reflex as claimed' and that 'the title is also not supported by the results.' While the reprogramming itself is accepted, the characterization as reflex-speed remains contested.

results.result: After reprogramming to the deflected rule, archerfish immediately generalized their decisions to novel untrained conditions including different height levels, prey sizes, and speeds. Fish turned accurately to deflected landing points appropriate for these new conditions without additional training, demonstrating that the new rule is represented abstractly rather than as a simple lookup table.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accepted the generalization findings without raising concerns. The editor noted these results as part of the 'convincing' data package, and Reviewer 3 explicitly praised the finding that 'fish learn in an impressive way the new rule' and can use it 'in a variety of novel situations that include height, side and speed of the prey.' After revision, reviewers confirmed 'the authors addressed the initial critiques adequately' regarding these generalization experiments.

results.result: The archerfish decision circuit can simultaneously operate on two distinct rules, using ballistic predictions for triangle-shaped objects and deflected predictions for disk-shaped objects. Fish appropriately selected which rule to apply based on object shape, even when shape information was available only during the brief decision phase after motion onset, with no differences in latency or kinematics between the two conditions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers uniformly accepted this dual-rule finding as a key result. The editor highlighted it as demonstrating the system 'can adapt to different simulated physics and different prey shapes.' Reviewer 3 called it 'a remarkable finding' that 'fish can master simultaneously two decision-making rules based on the different shape of objects.' No concerns were raised about the methodology or interpretation of these experiments, and the post-revision consensus confirmed adequate handling of any initial questions.

results.result: The archerfish high-speed decision lacks a speed-accuracy tradeoff and can be made in as little as 40 ms (or less than 100 ms more generally). There is no correlation between response latency and accuracy in either the original ballistic decisions or the reprogrammed deflected decisions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly challenged the 40 ms claim, stating 'there is little support for the 40 ms reaction time' and noting that previous studies (Schlegel 2008, Tsvilling 2012) show 60-75 ms latencies. The reviewer emphasized this is 'critical for the analysis' because the reflex-speed characterization depends on it, and criticized 'mentioning the 40 ms in the abstract is overselling the result.' While the lack of speed-accuracy tradeoff itself was not disputed, the specific timing claims that underpin the 'reflex-like' characterization were directly challenged and remain inadequately supported according to this reviewer.

results.result: The findings provide a counterexample to the prevailing view that high-speed decision-making is generally based on simplifying heuristics and lacks flexibility. High-speed decisions that lack a speed-accuracy tradeoff can offer learning capacities and cognitive aspects comparable to much slower decisions.
results.evaluation: The editor and Reviewer 3 endorsed this broad conclusion, with the editor stating the study 'should be of relevance to those interested in rapid decision making in general' and Reviewer 3 appreciating 'the idea conveyed by the authors that even stimuli triggering apparently hardwired responses can be relearned.' However, Reviewer 2's challenge to the reflex-speed characterization undermines this conclusion's foundation. The reviewer's concern that 'if the reaction time is longer, maybe this is not a reflex as claimed' and that 'the title is also not supported by the results' directly questions whether these decisions truly represent the high-speed category being contrasted with flexible cognition.

results.result: The study analyzed a group of six fish that reached homogeneous performance stages, though there could be individual differences in learning speed.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly raised concerns about individual variability, asking 'How were the individual performances in terms of consistency? Were all fish equally good in adjusting/learning the new rule? How did errors vary according to individual identity?' The reviewer noted this information 'should be available' and 'is essential for appreciating the flexibility of the system.' While the authors addressed these concerns in revision (as indicated by the consensus that critiques were 'adequately' handled), the small sample size and initial lack of individual-level analysis created uncertainty about the generalizability of the findings.

results.result: Learning the new deflected rule required more than 1750 presentations over 55 experimental days.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 specifically requested clarification about learning dynamics, asking 'how long did this process last? How many hours, days, weeks were needed for the fish to learn?' and stating 'learning dynamics is relevant to understanding the flexibility of the system.' While the manuscript provides the trial count and day count, the reviewer's concern about whether this information was 'explained in a proper way' suggests the temporal aspects of learning were not initially presented with sufficient clarity. The post-revision acceptance indicates this was addressed, but the initial presentation was inadequate.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the VR system validation (C49-C65). OpenEval finds the system SUPPORTED with robust controls and statistical validation. Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 2's concerns about 120 FPS frame rate producing 15mm jumps and questioning whether fish perceive continuous motion, though other reviewers found it sophisticated and post-revision the manuscript improved.

Peer review rates it UNCERTAIN - while accepting the reprogramming itself as 'remarkable,' Reviewer 2 challenges the foundational 40ms reaction time claim, arguing it relies on insufficient support and questioning the 'reflex-like' characterization that is central to the paper's framing.

Peer review also rates it SUPPORTED - all reviewers accepted these findings, with Reviewer 3 praising the 'impressive' learning and ability to use the rule 'in a variety of novel situations.'
